title: Common ancestor in a parent–child graph → earliest ancestor
label: single
statement:
Input: a list of `(parent, child)` pairs describing several generations; every person has a unique positive id. Write a function that takes the pairs and two people and returns **true if and only if they share at least one ancestor** (a parent, grandparent, and so on — a person is not their own ancestor).

```
pairs = [(1,3), (2,3), (3,6), (5,6), (5,7), (4,5), (15,21), (4,8), (4,9), (9,11), (14,4), (13,12), (12,9), (15,13)]
hasCommonAncestor(pairs, 3, 8)  → false      hasCommonAncestor(pairs, 6, 8)  → true
hasCommonAncestor(pairs, 1, 3)  → false      hasCommonAncestor(pairs, 7, 11) → true
hasCommonAncestor(pairs, 21, 11) → true
```
provenance: Reported on LeetCode Discuss for a LinkedIn interview on **13 Mar 2026** (in your list): Java internals discussion (Callable/Runnable, HashMap, ConcurrentHashMap, JVM), then this DSA question. Your list includes the full statement and 11 sample answers; all 11 are tests here. No LeetCode equivalent — it is a well-known interview question rather than a LeetCode problem. Stage 2 (earliest ancestor) is the usual follow-up, not reported here.

1.q: Is a person their own ancestor?
1.a: No — the samples prove it: (1, 3) is false.
A visited set — 9 is reachable from 4 and from 12.

2.a: O(n) to build the map, O(n) for each walk.

2.q: Many queries on the same family tree?
2.a: Precompute each person's ancestor set once (bitsets if ids are dense), then each query is a set intersection.

3.q: The family data changes while queries run.
3.a: Build an immutable map and swap it in, rather than locking every query.

4.a: Store parents in a key-value store; walk upward with a bounded BFS from both sides and stop at the first meet.

5.q: What did this round also cover?
5.a: Java internals — the C# equivalents are Task vs Thread, Dictionary internals (buckets, resize) and ConcurrentDictionary (lock striping).

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
- Is a person their own ancestor? (No — that is why (3, 6) is true via 1 and 2, but (1, 3) is false.)
- Can someone have two parents? (Yes — 3 has 1 and 2.)
- Can the same ancestor be reached by two routes? (Yes — use a visited set.)
- An id that never appears? (No ancestors → false.)

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md: Ancestors are just "walk upward". Build child → parents once, gather every ancestor of the first person into a set, then walk upward from the second person and stop at the first ancestor that is in the set.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md: I would say, before coding: "B."uild a child → parents map, collect every ancestor of one person by walking upward with a set, then walk upward from the other until an ancestor is found — O(n) time and memory."

learn.title: 12 · Common AI mistakes
learn.md:
- Building parent → children and searching downward — the wrong direction.
- Counting a person as their own ancestor (then (1, 3) would be true).
- No visited set: 9 is reached from both 4 and 12, so work repeats (and a bad input could loop).
- Recursion with no memo on a deep family tree.
